books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — The Jungle and the Meat-packing Industry
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpt (abridged) from the Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906, public domain.
stimulus.text: For the purposes hereinbefore set forth the Secretary shall cause to be made, by inspectors appointed for that purpose, an examination and inspection of all cattle, sheep, swine, and goats before they shall be allowed to enter into any slaughtering, packing, or canning establishment... and said inspectors shall have access at all times, by day or night, whether the establishment be operated or not, to every part of said establishment; and said inspectors shall mark, stamp, tag, or label as 'Inspected and passed' all such products found to be not adulterated. — Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: The inspection system described in the act relied on

options.text: voluntary self-regulation by the packing companies on their own
options.misconception: The act imposed mandatory federal inspection precisely because voluntary practices had failed.

options.text: federal inspectors inside plants stamping products 'Inspected and passed'
inspections conducted by the state governments, not the federal government
options.misconception: The inspectors were federal, appointed under the Secretary of Agriculture, not state officials.

options.text: an outright ban on all industrial meatpacking
options.misconception: The act regulated packing; it did not ban it, and the plants kept operating under inspection.

rationales.A: The act does not trust the packers to regulate themselves. It orders federal inspectors into the plants because voluntary practice had failed.
rationales.B: The act puts federal inspectors inside the plants, gives them access at all times by day or night, and lets their judgment carry a government stamp: 'Inspected and passed.' The mechanism is continuous federal presence plus an official seal.
rationales.C: The Secretary appoints the inspectors. The system is federal, not fifty state systems.
rationales.D: The act regulates meatpacking; it does not end it. The plants kept running, now under federal inspection.
rationales.general:
1. Read the mechanism. Inspectors appointed by the Secretary examine animals before slaughter and have access to every part of the plant, day or night.
2. Read the stamp. Products found not adulterated are marked 'Inspected and passed.'
3. Rule out the alternatives. The system is federal, mandatory, and regulatory, not voluntary, state-run, or a ban.
Remember: a law's mechanism is in its verbs, so read what the law tells its inspectors to do.
